name: Guduchi
doshaKarma: Commonly described as Tridoṣa-śāmaka; practical effect depends on indication, preparation and dose.
identification: Climbing plant with characteristic heart-shaped (cordate) leaves and a succulent green-to-grey-brown stem with prominent warty/tuberculated protuberances.
spotter: For practical identification, examine the cordate leaf together with the characteristic succulent, warty stem. Authenticate the botanical species before use because Tinospora species can be confused or substituted in trade.
formulations: Other compound preparations containing Guduchi (composition varies by text/edition)
dose: Use the dose specified for the particular classical formulation or pharmacopoeial preparation; there is no single universal dose for every preparation.
anupana: Preparation- and indication-dependent; select according to the relevant classical reference.
modern: Experimental research has investigated immunomodulatory, anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, antimicrobial, hepatoprotective and antidiabetic activities. These findings should not be treated as proof of clinical efficacy for a specific disease.
safety: Use authenticated material and an appropriate preparation. Published literature has raised concerns about liver injury reports associated with products sold as Guduchi/Giloy and about species substitution/adulteration. Tinospora crispa is hepatotoxic; botanical authentication is therefore important. The relationship between authentic T. cordifolia and reported autoimmune-like hepatitis remains debated.
researchGaps: Standardization of plant part and extract
classicalReferences: Guduchi is described across classical Ayurvedic Samhitas and Nighantus. Exact śloka numbers should be verified against the specific edition before being entered in the library.
modernReferences: Ayurvedic and pharmacognostic reviews of Tinospora cordifolia

name: Yaṣṭimadhu
prabhava: Classical descriptions emphasize soothing and nourishing actions; verify Prabhava wording against the chosen text/edition.
doshaKarma: Predominantly Vāta-Pitta śāmaka; excessive use may increase Kapha.
identification: Elongated cylindrical root; yellowish interior; characteristic sweet taste. The plant has pinnate leaves and pale purple/blue flowers.
spotter: For practical identification, combine the sweet taste and characteristic root appearance with botanical morphology rather than identifying a commercial root from taste alone.
formulations: Formulation names and compositions should be checked against the specific classical text or pharmacopoeia
dose: Dose is formulation- and preparation-dependent; use the relevant classical or pharmacopoeial monograph rather than a universal dose.
modern: Research has investigated gastroprotective, anti-inflammatory, antioxidant and antimicrobial effects. Evidence varies by extract, preparation and study design.
safety: Prolonged or high intake of glycyrrhizin-containing liquorice may cause sodium retention, hypokalemia and raised blood pressure. Duration, dose, formulation and patient factors matter.
researchGaps: Clinical evidence for specific Ayurvedic indications
classicalReferences: Yaṣṭimadhu is described in classical Ayurvedic literature. Exact śloka numbers should be verified against the specific edition before being entered in the library.
modernReferences: Pharmacognostic and pharmacological reviews of Glycyrrhiza glabra
